newsitem.title: USA: Cook Inlet lease sale nets $3.1 million in bids.
newsitem.headline: Cook Inlet lease sale nets $3.1 million in bids.

text.p: A controversial oil and gas lease sale for about one million acres in Cook Inlet and the adjacent Kenai Peninsula netted $3.1 million Wednesday for the state of Alaska, according to prelimary figures released by officials.

Bidding was especially heavy for tracts in both the western edge of the inlet, where prospects for finding new oil are believed to be high, and for onshore sections of the southern Kenai Peninsula, prospective sites for new gas discoveries.

Alaska Natural Resources Commissioner John Shively said the sale demonstrated renewed industry interest in the state after a period of doldrums that included ill will over the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill and worries about declining production at the North Slope's Prudhoe Bay.
"I think the governor's (pro-industry) message is getting out," he said.
Alaska Division of Oil and Gas Director Ken Boyd also hailed the sale results as a sign that oil companies want to explore more of the state.
"You told us that if we made the land available that you would buy it, and you've proved that here today," he told industry representatives after reading the bids.

But environmentalists, fishermen and many Kenai Peninsula residents bitterly opposed the lease sale and pleaded unsuccessfully with Gov. Tony Knowles to stop it or excise the most controversial tracts from it.

"I think that Governor Knowles will probably live to regret this sale, politically. I think that it was a very poor public process," said Jay Stange, an environmental activist who attended Wednesday's lease sale.

He was unimpressed with Knowles' announcement Tuesday that any sensitive tracts winning bids would be slapped with a 90-day permit moratorium to allow residents, fishermen and other interested parties time to work out compromises with potential developers.
"He may hold up permit decisions. But the fact is that in eight years the three oil companies that operate platforms in Cook Inlet have violated their permits 4,200 times," Stange said.

Cook Inlet is the site of Alaska's oldest operating oil and gas fields. But most activity has been concentrated on the northern part of the inlet. Residents have rejected oil development in the southern part of the inlet, which is famous for its salmon runs and tourist attractions.
Oil companies appeared undeterred by the controversy.
Especially active in the bidding were Unocal and Miami-based Forcenergy, companies that on Tuesday announced an alliance to expand Cook Inlet exploration. The companies bid on tracts as partners.
Also winning rights to explore several tracts were Anadarko Petroleum and Arco Alaska Inc., which bid as partners.

Other successful bidders were Marathon Oil; Union Texas Petroleum, Syracuse, New York-based Frontier Petroleum Corp.; Soldotna, Alaska-based Gas-Pro Alaska; Houston-based Aurora Gas; and two individuals, according to preliminary results.
